newsitem.title: USA: Ford dealers intrigued by consolidation proposal.
newsitem.headline: Ford dealers intrigued by consolidation proposal.

text.p: Ford and Lincoln-Mercury dealers in Indianapolis said Monday they are intrigued by Ford Motor Co.'s proposal to create a single dealership entity for the entire metropolitan area.

But the success of the bold plan -- viewed as one of the most ambitious shake-ups of the traditional franchised dealer system in decades -- hinges on the amount of cash that dealers receive for their property, they say.

Ford executives last week briefed dealers on the voluntary plan, which calls for the consolidation of about 18 Indianapolis-area Ford and Lincoln-Mercury dealerships into five or six giant sales outlets and several stand-alone, satellite service facilities that could handle light repairs and warranty work.
The new locations would be owned by a single entity partly owned by Ford and by the participating dealers, said Ford spokesman John Ochs.

"It's ploughing absolutely new ground," said Jerry Harvey, president of Paul Harvey Ford in Indianapolis. "I think generally speaking, the dealers are supportive, but we don't know what they're going to offer us."
Dealers said Ford officials estimated costs for dealer buy-outs and new construction costs at $155 million, but Ochs said the automaker has not disclosed any costs for the project.
While Ford won't force the plan on dealers, Ochs said the company is looking to test the concept in two to three medium-sized markets in the next two to three years.
Dealers said Ford also will consider a public offering in the new distribution entity if the plan proves successful in the test cities.

Publicly traded car dealer groups have gone on a buying spree in the past year, driving dealership selling prices to record levels. Most notable among them has been H. Wayne Huizenga's Republic Industries Inc., which is building the AutoNation used-car superstore chain.

AutoNation, Circuit City Stores Inc.'s CarMax and others are using many of the customer-friendly techniques pioneered by General Motors Corp.'s Saturn unit, including salaried sales consultants, no-haggle pricing and large selections of high-quality vehicles.
Both GM and Chrysler Corp. have had programmes to reduce their dealership ranks through consolidation and buy-outs, but neither has proposed as radical a restructuring of their distribution system.

Analysts view Ford's move as a response to the growth of the superstores, which automakers fear may exert more control over auto retailing in the future. Wesley Brown, an automotive consultant with Nextrend Inc. in Thousand Oaks, Calif., said Ford will benefit from gaining more control over its dealers.

"As a manufacturer, you gain control over the sales and customer satisfaction processes," Brown said. "Now what you have is a bunch of dealers competing against one another. I think this occurrence in Indianapolis is going to be the beginning of a trend."
Dealer participation hinges on cash, particularly since many regularly turn down buyout offers from larger dealer groups.
"Show me the money," said an Indianapolis Ford dealer who spoke on condition of anonymity. "It all hinges on the money."
Joseph Myers, owner of Collins Lincoln-Mercury, said he believes Ford is "right-on with their concept," but adds that it could displace a lot of dealership employees in the long run.
"Our people are very concerned for what it all means, he said. "You're talking about people's livelihoods."
Ford plans to begin discussing the proposal with individual dealers in Indianapolis in about two weeks.
